items.q: For f(x) = x^2 with x in R, what is the range?
hints: Think about the smallest value x^2 can take, and whether it has an upper limit.
x^2 is never negative, and can be made as large as you like, so y ranges from 0 upwards.

items.q: For f(x) = 1/x, what is the domain?
hints: Think about which input value would make the function undefined.
Dividing by x is impossible when x = 0.

items.q: For x in [0,3], f(x) = 2x + 1. What is the range?
hints: Since f is increasing, evaluate f at each end of the domain.
f(0) = 1 and f(3) = 7, and f increases steadily between them.

items.q: For f(x) = sqrt(x), what is the domain?
hints: Think about which input values give a real square root.
The square root of a negative number is not real, so x cannot be negative.

items.q: For f(x) = x + 4, what is the domain if no restriction is given?
hints: Think about whether any input value would cause a problem for this function.
Adding 4 works for every real x, with no undefined cases.
All real numbers

items.q: For f(x) = (x - 2)^2, what is the minimum value in the range?
hints: A squared expression is smallest when the bracket is zero.
(x-2)^2 is smallest when x = 2, giving (0)^2.

items.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, find f(g(3)).
hints: Work from the inside out: find g(3) first, then apply f to that result.

items.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, find g(f(x)).
hints: Substitute the whole expression f(x) into g in place of x.

items.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, find f(g(x)).
hints: Substitute the whole expression g(x) into f in place of x.

items.q: If f(x) = x - 4 and g(x) = 3x, find f(g(2)).
hints: Work from the inside out: find g(2) first, then apply f to that result.

items.q: If f(x) = x + 5 and g(x) = 2x, find g(f(1)).
hints: Work from the inside out: find f(1) first, then apply g to that result.

items.q: If f(x) = x^2 and g(x) = x + 1, find f(g(2)).
hints: Work from the inside out: find g(2) first, then apply f to that result.

items.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, solve f(g(x)) = 9 for x (positive value only).
hints: Write f(g(x)) as an expression in x, set it equal to 9, then solve.

items.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x - 4.
hints: Write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

items.q: For f(x) = 3x - 4, find f^-1(11).
hints: Use the inverse formula f^-1(x) = (x + 4)/3.

items.q: What condition must a function satisfy to have an inverse on its full domain?
hints: Think about what would go wrong if two different inputs gave the same output.
If two inputs shared an output, the inverse wouldn't know which one to send it back to — so the function must be one-to-one.
It must be one-to-one

items.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = x + 7.
hints: Write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.
x = y + 7, so y = x - 7.

items.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 3.
hints: Write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

items.q: True or false: a many-to-one function has an inverse on the full domain.
hints: Think about whether the inverse would know which of several inputs to return.
A many-to-one function sends several inputs to the same output, so reversing it is ambiguous.
False

items.q: Why does y = x^2 not have an inverse on all real x?
hints: Think about whether two different x-values could give the same y-value.
Both x = 2 and x = -2 give y = 4, so the function isn't one-to-one over all reals.
It is not one-to-one

items.q: If y = x^2 with x >= 0, find the inverse.
hints: Swap x and y, then take the square root — remembering the restriction keeps only the positive root.
x = y^2 with y >= 0, so y = sqrt(x).
y = sqrt(x)

items.q: If y = (x - 2)^2 with x >= 2, find the inverse.
hints: Swap x and y, take the square root (positive, since x >= 2), then rearrange.
x = (y-2)^2 with y >= 2, so sqrt(x) = y - 2.
y = 2 + sqrt(x)

items.q: If y = (x + 3)^2 with x >= -3, find the inverse.
hints: Swap x and y, take the square root (positive, since x >= -3), then rearrange.
x = (y+3)^2 with y >= -3, so sqrt(x) = y + 3.
y = -3 + sqrt(x)

items.q: What restriction on x makes y = x^2 invertible?
hints: Think about splitting the graph of y = x^2 so each half is one-to-one.
Restricting to only the non-negative or only the non-positive x-values makes the function one-to-one.
x >= 0 or x <= 0

items.q: True or false: restricting the domain can make a quadratic invertible.
hints: Think about what happens to a many-to-one graph when you only keep half of it.
Keeping only x >= 0 (or only x <= 0) removes the repeated outputs, making it one-to-one.
True

items.q: Write the graph y = x^2 shifted up 3.
items.imageAlt: The graph of y = x squared (dashed) and the same curve shifted up 3 units (solid). The equation of the shifted curve is unknown.
items.imageCaption: Solid curve: y = x² shifted up 3.
hints: Shifting a graph up by a adds a to the whole function.

items.q: Write the graph y = x^2 shifted right 4.
hints: Shifting a graph right by a replaces x with (x - a).

items.q: Write the graph y = x^2 reflected in the x-axis.
items.imageAlt: The graph of y = x squared (dashed) and the same curve reflected in the x-axis (solid). The equation of the reflected curve is unknown.
hints: Reflecting in the x-axis negates the whole function.

items.q: Write the graph y = sqrt(x) shifted left 2.
hints: Shifting a graph left by a replaces x with (x + a).
y = sqrt(x + 2).
y = sqrt(x + 2)

items.q: Write the graph y = x^2 shifted down 5.
hints: Shifting a graph down by a subtracts a from the whole function.

items.q: Write the graph y = x^3 reflected in the y-axis.
hints: Reflecting in the y-axis replaces x with -x.

items.q: Write the graph y = x^2 shifted right 3 and up 2.
hints: Apply both shifts together: replace x with (x - 3) for the rightward shift, and add 2 for the upward shift.

items.q: Solve: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
hints: Factorise into two brackets whose constants multiply to 6 and add to -5.
x = 2 or x = 3

items.q: Simplify: (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3).
hints: Factorise the numerator as a difference of two squares.
(x^2 - 9) = (x - 3)(x + 3), so the (x - 3) factors cancel.

items.q: Solve: x^2 - 4 < 0.
hints: Find where x^2 - 4 = 0 first, then decide which side of those roots makes it negative.
x^2 - 4 = 0 at x = -2 and x = 2; between them the expression is negative.

items.q: Factorise: x^2 + 7x + 10.
hints: Find two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7.
5 and 2 multiply to 10 and add to 7.

items.q: Solve: x^2 + x - 12 = 0.
hints: Find two numbers that multiply to -12 and add to 1.
x = 3 or x = -4

items.q: Solve: x^2 - x - 6 >= 0.
hints: Find the roots of x^2 - x - 6 = 0 first, then decide which side of those roots makes it non-negative.
(x - 3)(x + 2) = 0 gives x = 3 or x = -2; outside these roots the expression is positive.

items.q: How does the angle at the centre compare with the angle at the circumference on the same arc?
hints: Recall the circle theorem linking the centre and circumference angles on the same arc.
The angle at the centre is always twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
It is double

items.q: What do opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to?
hints: Recall the circle theorem for a quadrilateral with all four vertices on the circle.
Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

items.q: What angle is formed between a tangent and a radius at the point of contact?
hints: Recall the circle theorem about tangents and radii.
A tangent always meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle.

items.q: Angles in the same segment are what?
hints: Recall the circle theorem about angles subtended by the same arc from the same side.
All angles in the same segment, standing on the same arc, are equal to each other.
Equal

items.q: The angle in a semicircle is always what?
hints: Recall the circle theorem for an angle subtended by a diameter.
Any angle in a semicircle, standing on the diameter, is a right angle.

items.q: True or false: the alternate segment angle equals the angle between the tangent and chord.
hints: Recall the alternate segment theorem.
The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
True

items.q: A cyclic quadrilateral has opposite angles x and 100°. The angle at the centre stands on the same arc as x. Find the centre angle.
hints: Find x first using the cyclic quadrilateral rule, then double it for the centre angle.
x = 180 - 100 = 80, so the centre angle = 2 x 80.

items.q: If P(A) = 0.35, find P(not A).
hints: Use P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

items.q: A fair die is rolled. Find the probability of a prime number.
hints: List the prime numbers on a die, then count them out of 6.
Primes on a die: 2, 3, 5 — that's 3 out of 6 outcomes.

items.q: Two coins are tossed. Find the probability of exactly one head.
hints: List all four equally likely outcomes, then count how many have exactly one head.
Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT — exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, 2 out of 4.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. Find P(red).
hints: P(red) = number of red counters / total counters.

items.q: True or false: probabilities must be between 0 and 1 inclusive.
hints: Recall the valid range for any probability.
0 means impossible and 1 means certain — every probability lies between them.
True

items.q: If events are mutually exclusive, what is P(A and B)?
hints: Think about what 'mutually exclusive' means for two events happening together.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time, so their overlap is impossible.

items.q: A bag has 12 balls: red, blue, and green. P(red) = 1/3 and P(blue) = 1/4. Find P(green).
hints: All the probabilities must add up to 1.
